setting: A fictional short talk to colleagues at a monthly team lunch, introduced by a friendly host.

presentation.situation: {{host}} has invited you to give a two-minute talk at the team lunch about {{topic}}. Use your own ideas and examples. Speak in a few longer turns: open with why it matters, give your main points, and finish with what you want people to do. Then take one question.
presentation.opening: Thanks, everyone. Our speaker today is going to talk about {{topic}}. The floor is yours. Why should we care about this?

brief.you_are: You are giving a short talk to about twenty colleagues at a team lunch.
brief.situation: Your topic is {{topic}}. The audience is friendly and busy, and they have not prepared anything. {{host}} is hosting, and will ask you one question at the end.
brief.task: Open by saying why this matters to them, give two or three clear points with an example, and finish by asking them to do one thing. Then answer the question.
brief.done_looks_like: People know why it matters, can repeat your main points, and know the one thing you want them to do.

participants.name: You
goals: Give a clear, memorable short talk

participants.name: {{host}}
participants.relationship: Hosts the monthly team lunch and introduces the speakers

card.want: A short, useful talk that the audience will remember, finishing on time.
card.hidden_need: Wants the speaker to do well, and the lunch to feel worthwhile.
card.attitude: Warm and encouraging, and keeps an eye on the time. Listens more than speaks.
card.speech: Friendly and very brief. Gives the speaker the floor. Never gives a talk of their own, and never comments on the speaker's English.
tactics: Say very little between parts of the talk
Ask one audience-style question at the end

pressure.gentle: Encouraging, with an easy final question.
pressure.balanced: Mentions time once, and asks a real question.
pressure.challenging: Asks a sceptical question from the audience.

ledger.text: The talk is about {{topic}}, and should last about two minutes.
About twenty colleagues are listening over lunch.
The details and examples in the talk come from the speaker. The host does not supply them.

objectives.description: Open with why it matters to this audience
objectives.evidence: The learner begins by connecting the topic to the listeners, not with apologies or a long introduction.
alternatives: Most of us lose an hour a day to this, so here's how to get it back

objectives.description: Organize main points with an example
objectives.evidence: The learner gives clearly separated points, with at least one concrete example.

objectives.description: Close with one clear call to action
objectives.evidence: The learner ends by summing up or asking the audience to do one specific thing.
alternatives: So tomorrow, try one thing: block your first hour

examples: Most of us have had this problem ...
So here's one thing to try this week ...
prerequisites: Think of one real example you could use.

beats.goal: The speaker opens by showing why this matters to the audience.
signals: \b(?:most of us|all of us|each of you|you (?:may|might|probably)|have you ever|imagine|why (?:this|it) matters|matters (?:to|for)|every day|we all)\b
opportunity: Before you go further, why does this matter to the people in this room?
Go on. What's in it for us?
beats.orient: You're giving a short talk, and I'm the host. Your topic is {{topic}}. Start by telling everyone why it matters to them.
fallback: Go ahead. Why does this matter to us?

beats.goal: The speaker gives main points. The host keeps quiet.
signals: \b(?:first|second|third|another|for example|for instance|my main point|one thing|the next)\b
opportunity: Thanks. What are your main points?
Can you give us an example of that?
beats.orient: Now give your main points. Two is plenty. Say 'first' and 'second', and give an example from your own experience.
fallback: Can you give us an example?

beats.goal: The speaker ends with what they want the audience to do.
signals: \b(?:so (?:try|tomorrow|this week|next time|please|my advice|remember)|in (?:short|summary|conclusion)|to (?:sum|finish|close)|i'?d like you to|i (?:ask|encourage) you|one thing to|try this|remember)\b
opportunity: We're nearly out of time. What's the one thing you'd like us to do?
How would you like to finish?
beats.orient: Time to finish. Tell everyone the one thing you'd like them to do after this talk.
fallback: What's the one thing you'd like us to do?
We're nearly out of time. How would you like to finish?

closing_line: Thank you, that was really useful. Let's give our speaker a round of applause.

o1.good: Beginning with the audience's own experience, so they have a reason to listen.
common_mistakes: Apologizing or saying you are nervous
o1.micro_lesson: Your first sentence should be about them, not you.
o1.model: Most of us lose an hour a day to this, so here's how to get it back.
o1.smaller_step: Say one reason this matters to the people in the room.

o2.good: Few points, clearly marked, with a real example people can remember.
o2.micro_lesson: People remember examples. Use 'first' and 'second' so they can follow you.
o2.model: First, block the first hour. For example, I stopped checking email until ten.
o2.smaller_step: Give one point and say: for example.

o3.good: Ending on one action, rather than letting the talk fade out.
common_mistakes: Adding a new point at the end
o3.micro_lesson: The last thing you say is what people remember. Make it one action.
o3.model: So tomorrow, try one thing: block your first hour.
o3.smaller_step: Say one thing you want them to try.

variants.topic: one habit that makes your working day better
something you learned from a mistake at work
how to run a shorter, better meeting
